Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00271

The imaginal human being also judges things through its own being, whether these judgments come from imagination or another inner power. It desires what is pleasant and feels anger toward what conflicts with it. It does not need a separate desire or anger added to it. The same is true of the intellectual human being in all the corresponding ways.
Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00272

The greatest of the philosophers says: “These senses are weak intellects, and those intellects are strong senses.” Someone might object: if the human being in the higher world can sense, and sensation is what distinguishes animals, then sensation must be a reaction to a physical form. How can a noble, higher being have a sense that belongs to a lower one?
Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00273

The answer, as we learn from the philosopher, is that the relation between ordinary sense and intellectual sense is like the relation between a flesh-and-blood animal and the intellectual animal. The same is true of what is sensed here and what is sensed in the higher world. The sense found in this lower world is not like the sense found in the higher one: there, the sense is directed toward things that are themselves higher. That is why the sight of this lower animal is connected to the sight of the higher animal.
Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00274

I say that the same is true of hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Their connection is like the connection between material things and their intellectual forms in the higher world, and in God's eternal knowledge.
Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00275

The Prophet, peace be upon him and his family, said that this fire had been washed seventy times with water before it was brought down to us. This points to the fact that the fire we know is one stage in the descent of an intellectual fire. The Prophet also said that he spent the night with his Lord, who fed him and gave him drink. He said, “I can smell the Breath of the All-Merciful coming from Yemen.” He said, “The earth was gathered and folded up for me, and I saw its eastern and western ends.” He also said, “God placed His hand on my shoulder, and I felt the coolness of it between my breasts.” These reports describe perception through the subtle senses of the next life, not through the ordinary senses that wear out.
Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00276

The Prophet also said, “The sky groans, and it has every right to groan: there is no space in it the size of a foot without an angel bowing or prostrating.” In short, the intellectual human being shines its light on the lower, bodily human being through the imaginal human being, which stands between them.
Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00277

The soul's effect on an image already present within it is like sunlight falling on a body in one way, but different in another. The sun makes an object visible; the soul brings its own imagined forms into being. When the soul imagines something, it gives rise to its image in its own world, not in the outer world, and perceives it through its own being, not through another image.
Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00278

The soul also perceives things that are visible outside it. As we explained earlier in our discussion of sight, the material thing and its position in relation to the eye prepare the soul to bring forth an image like that thing. The image is separate from matter and its material conditions, and exists in the soul's own realm, like an imagined image. The difference is that an image of something seen depends on an outside object and its conditions, while an imagined image does not.
Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00279
Chapter 8 — What the soul first connects to
Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00280

The soul acts on the body's dense, material organs only through a suitable medium that connects the two. This medium is a fine, light substance called the spirit. It flows through the organs by way of the nerves in the brain. The claim that the soul first acts through this spirit—said to be formed from the finer, vaporous part of the bodily fluids, while the body is formed from their thicker, coarser part—is close to obvious and needs no proof. The levels of existence are arranged from fine to coarse, just as they are arranged from noble to low.
Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00281

Within an animal, one part is finer than the rest. This is the vital spirit carried in the arteries. Another part is coarser than the rest, near the hip. Between the finest and the coarsest are suitable intermediate levels, arranged one above another by God's wise design, like the layers of the heavenly bodies and the elements.
Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00282

The finer a thing is in its substance, the more actively it acts and the less it is acted on. The coarser it is, the more it is acted on and the less it acts. For example, the body's vital spirit naturally acts on the blood, which belongs to the same level as itself. The blood in turn acts on the moisture of the brain, and that moisture acts on the muscles. This continues from one part to another until it reaches the hardest parts, which are wholly receptive and do not act on anything else.
Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00283

The same order should be understood among spiritual beings, just as we understand it among bodily things. The same is true of the great world, as it is of the small world of the human being. Among bodily things, one part is the finest—the highest celestial sphere—and another is the coarsest—the earth below. Between them are orderly stages, each between the finer and the coarser, set in place by divine wisdom.
Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00284

The evidence shows that the finer a thing is, the more it acts; the coarser it is, the more it receives. This is why prayers turn toward the sky when people ask for what they need, seek good things, or ask for their prayers to be answered. In truth, turning toward the sky means turning toward God. This is also what some mystics mean when they say that God's light is one, but appears in different forms according to the places where it shines. The being that flows from God is one in its reality, though it has different levels according to how near or far it is from Him.
Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00285

Once we understand this, we can see that the soul belongs to the world of pure intellectual light, while the body is dense, dark, and material. The soul cannot act on the body in a way that makes them one natural thing unless there is a medium between them. That medium is the fine substance doctors call the spirit. There is also a suitable medium between each of these levels and the one next to it. For example, an imaginal, intermediate form lies between the rational soul and the animal spirit, while pure, fine blood lies between that spirit and the body.
Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00286

There is evidence that this substance, called the spirit, exists. If the nerves are blocked, sensation and movement stop beyond the blockage, on the side away from the brain. The blockage prevents only the passage of bodily substances. Medical experience also shows that an abundance of spirit brings joy, energy, strength, courage, and desire. A lack of it brings epilepsy, fainting, grief, sadness, and melancholy. If it leaves the heart, death comes suddenly. The soul is connected to the body through this spirit. And since the soul is one, it must first connect to one organ through this subtle spirit, then reach the brain, liver, and other organs through that first organ.
Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00287

People disagree about which organ is the main one, giving life and power to the rest: the heart or the brain. Most doctors and natural philosophers say it is the heart. It is the warmest part of the body, while the brain is not. The heart is therefore the right place for the warm, inborn spirit.
Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00288

Also, intense thinking heats the brain. If the brain were not cool by nature, it might burn when the heat of the spirit and the heat of thought came together. The heart is also the first organ to form, the first to move, and the last to stop. So it is the soul's first point of connection to the body. From there, it reaches the brain, the liver, and the other organs in order.
Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00289

One might object: if the heart is the main organ and the source that gives the others their powers, and the soul's spirits flow from it to the brain, then the nerves should begin in the heart, not in the brain. Tools should begin at their source, not at the place that receives them. But the nerves begin in the brain, so the claim about the heart must be wrong.
Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00290

We answer that some commentators on the Canon of Medicine say no conclusive proof has ever shown that the nerves begin in the brain. Even setting that claim aside, someone could deny that a tool must begin at the source of its power. Why could a tool not begin in the organ that receives its power, after the power has reached it from the source? The spirits that carry the powers of sensation and movement could then pass through the brain.
Book Eight — Refuting the idea that souls move from one body to another, and answering its proponents
passage-en-00291
A full treatment of this question belongs in medical books.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00292
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00293
Some of the soul's powers exist at a higher level than others and are less open to division. This book has several chapters.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00294
Chapter 1 — The human being's distinctive traits
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00295

One distinctive human trait is speech. Consider the wisdom God showed in making human beings from the elements: He gave them a system of words shared by agreement. We need others to live in this world and depend on help from our own kind. If one person lived alone, with no one else of the same kind or family around, and no access to anything beyond what nature provided, that person would soon die or live badly.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00296

We need things that nature does not provide in a ready-to-use form, such as prepared food and made clothing. Natural food is not suitable for us to eat until it is prepared, and natural coverings are not useful until human work turns them into clothes. We need to learn crafts to live well. But one person cannot do every kind of work. People must help each other: one bakes bread for another, someone else weaves cloth, another carries goods, and each gives a share of their work in return.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00297

For these and similar reasons, we need a way to tell another person what is in our mind. The best way is with sound. Sound can be divided into letters and joined into many combinations without putting strain on the body. We already need to make sounds in order to breathe and cool the heart. Sound also does not last; it disappears as soon as it is made, so it does not remain for someone who has no need to hear it. A gesture can also communicate, but it is less useful: it can guide only someone who sees it from a particular direction, and the person making it must keep moving the eyes to direct it. Gesture is therefore less useful and takes more effort. Sound has none of these limits. So nature gave the human soul the ability to combine sounds and use them to communicate what is in the mind. This became our shared system of words.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00298

Other animals do not need speech in the same way. They find food in nature or need little work to prepare it; they come with their own coverings, such as skin and hair, or shelter in holes and caves. They still make sounds, and some of their calls show a little thought and tell others something of their feelings. But these calls give only a broad signal, enough to seek what is pleasant or avoid what is harmful. Human speech gives much more detail. We need to express almost endlessly many things, but we could not be born with a different sound for each one. So we need to create words and agree on their meanings.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00299

Another remarkable human trait is the ability to invent unusual crafts. Animals also build, especially birds, and bees build their hexagonal cells. A hexagon holds more space than other shapes after the circle, and resembles a circle in how much space it encloses. Bees do not use circles because gaps would be left between the cells. Squares would leave wasted corners inside. Their cells therefore fit together closely in a shape suited to their builder.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00300

Even so, animals do not invent these crafts through their own individual reasoning. Otherwise, their work would vary from one animal to another. Instead, their work follows an inspiration or guidance given by the beings that govern their kind, such as the angels. Most of these crafts serve the whole kind or some other kind, such as human beings, who seem to be the special purpose of animal life and its crafts. Only a small part of an animal's craft serves that particular animal. Human beings are different, especially those who have reached their full development: what each one does and makes serves that person's own life. Each person can continue as an individual in the next life and through their own intellect, while other animals continue as a kind, not as separate individuals.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00301

Another human trait is that unusual things can make us feel wonder and then laugh, while painful things can make us feel distress and then cry. Human beings also learn to take part in one another's interests. They are taught from childhood not to do certain things and to do others. This makes them firmly believe they ought to avoid one kind of act and choose another, for the sake of a well-ordered life. By God's care, they call the first kind shameful and the other good and beautiful.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00302

Other animals may also avoid certain acts. A trained lion, for example, may not eat its keeper, and a noble horse may not mate with its mother. But this does not come from a belief about right and wrong. Every animal naturally loves what suits and pleases it. It may grow attached to the person who feeds it and so refuse to eat that person. A horse raised by its mother from birth may grow so attached to her that this keeps it from mating with her. Other habits may come from an inspiration given to the animal, such as the love every animal feels for its young.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00303

If a person realizes that someone else has seen them do something shameful, they feel embarrassment. A person may also think that something harmful will happen in the future and feel fear, or think that something good will happen and feel hope. Other animals usually feel these things only in response to what is happening now. If they prepare for something, they do not do so because they clearly understand what may happen later. They act through an instinct given to their kind, as when ants quickly carry grain into their nest before rain. Perhaps they imagine some harm or rain is coming, just as an animal runs from an enemy because it imagines it will be struck. Or perhaps they are guided by an inspiration from the angel that governs their kind.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00304
In general, human actions that show judgment and reason come from each human being as an individual. In other animals, they come from a general plan for the kind.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00305

A human being can also think about future choices and decide whether to act. At one time, the person does what their judgment recommends; at another time, they hold back, even from something they could do before, because their judgment has changed. Other animals cannot do this. They have fixed patterns of behavior, whether or not those patterns lead to good results.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00306
Another human trait is recalling things that have left the mind. Other animals cannot do this in the same way; they do not deliberately bring back and think over what they once knew.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00307

The most distinctively human ability is to grasp general meanings fully apart from matter, as we have explained in our discussion of intellect and intelligible things. We can also use what we already know to discover what we do not yet know, both by reasoning about facts and by forming ideas. Most distinctively of all, some human souls can join the divine world so completely that they let go of their own self and live through God. Then God becomes their hearing, sight, hand, and foot, and they take on God's qualities.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00308

These are some of the human being's traits. Some belong to the body, but they occur through the soul, as with laughter and tears. Some are states of the soul that arise through the body, such as fear, hope, embarrassment, and grief. Others are purely intellectual, such as the theoretical and practical wisdom of the soul. Among all created beings, and especially among animals, the human being gathers together bodily, soulful, and intellectual qualities.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00309

Avicenna says that a human being deals with particular matters and general matters. We can form beliefs only about general matters. Even when we believe in a general way how a house should be built, that belief alone does not directly produce a particular house. Actions deal with particular things and come from particular parts of us.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00310

So a person must have one power that works with general ideas and another that thinks about particular choices: what should or should not be done, what helps or harms, and what is good or bad. This power uses reasoning and thought, whether sound or mistaken. It produces a judgment about one possible action in the future. People do not deliberate about what must happen or cannot happen, or about something that has already happened.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00311

When this power reaches a decision, it moves the power of desire, which moves the body. Or the practical power may draw on the power that handles general ideas, taking its general premises from it. The example is: “Every good act should be done; telling the truth is good; therefore, telling the truth should be done.” The practical power then applies that general judgment to a particular case: “This is telling the truth; telling the truth should be done; therefore, this should be done.” Theoretical and practical reason are two levels of one intellect, not two separate beings.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00312

The first power is called theoretical reason, because it seeks knowledge. The second is called practical reason, because it guides action. Theoretical reason deals with truth and falsehood; practical reason with good and bad in particular cases. The first deals with what is necessary, possible, or impossible; the second with what is good, shameful, or allowed. The first begins from first principles; the second usually begins from widely accepted views, claims people accept, or experience that may not be fully reliable.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00313

Each of these two powers has its own belief and judgment. A firm belief is a conclusion held as certain. A leaning belief allows that the opposite may still be true. Not everyone who leans toward a view believes it firmly, just as sensing is not the same as thinking, and imagining is not the same as forming a judgment. A human being therefore has a judge of sense, a judge of imagination, a judge of theory, and a judge of practical matters. The powers that move the body include imagination, practical reason, desire, and anger. Animals have three of these kinds of judgment.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00314

Practical reason needs the body and bodily powers in all its actions. Theoretical reason also needs the body and its powers, but not always or in every way; it can sometimes stand on its own. Neither of these powers alone is the human soul. The soul is the single being that has them. It is a single substance, ready for different actions—some that require bodily tools and full attention to them, and others that require no tools at all. We will explain this in its proper place.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00315

There are many points in Avicenna's account that could be questioned, but that would take too long to discuss here. What we have explained about the soul—its nature, stages, and unified existence across its different levels—is enough for a thoughtful reader. If we think carefully about Avicenna's claim that a person has a judge of sense, imagination, theory, and practical reason, we can see that the soul itself is all these powers. It is not merely a thing that owns them.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00316

Everyone knows that each person is one being with one self, and that all their actions come from this one being. Still, anyone who has studied the subject knows that a judge of sense must belong to the level of sense and what is sensed, and a judge of imagination must belong to the level of imagination. The practical judge belongs to the level of an immaterial power connected to particular images, as we explained in our discussion of imagination and imagined things. The theoretical judge belongs to the level of the intellect that is separate from matter.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00317

This shows that the soul develops from one stage to another in its very being, as we have claimed. Avicenna's further point—that the intellect needs the body and its powers at first, but can later stand on its own—also supports our view that the soul begins with the body and survives as a spirit. Avicenna does not accept the deep change in the soul's being that we have described. For the soul's need for the body is not like a craftsperson's need for a workshop for some extra task. At first, it needs the body and its powers in order to exist. The soul itself is a way of existing, not something added to a completed self.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00318

Once the soul becomes an active intellect, no longer needing the body, it becomes one of the beings of the intellectual world, like intelligible forms that understand themselves whether or not another being understands them. How could a bodily, material form become a form that can be understood in itself, whether or not someone thinks of it? It can do so only by changing and growing stronger in its very being, moving from the lowest stages to the highest. This is what is shown by the Prophet's ascent, as he passed through every level until he reached the highest and saw the greatest signs of his Lord.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00319

The same is shown by Abraham's vision: “We showed Abraham the kingdom of the heavens and the earth,” and by his words, “I have turned my face toward the One who created the heavens and the earth.” How could the human stage described by the words “I am only a human being like you” be the same as the divine stage described by the Prophet's saying, “I have a time with God when no angel brought near or prophet sent can reach me”?
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00320
Chapter 2 — The main qualities of the soul and the roots of good and bad character
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00321

Most differences in human character come from differences in the soul's strength and nobility, or in its weakness and baseness. We have already seen that existence itself has different degrees of strength and weakness, and that these differences change the nature and qualities of things.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00322

Human souls vary greatly in completeness, nobility, and deficiency. A strong soul can carry out great actions in many different areas. This is because it gathers many levels of existence within itself. A weak soul cannot do as much.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00323

We see weak souls that can attend to only one thing at a time. When they focus on thought, their senses grow weak; when they focus on their senses, their thought falters. If they devote themselves to moving the body, their ability to perceive is disrupted. Other souls are strong enough to combine different kinds of perception and action, especially the inner qualities that make up good character.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00324

Strength and weakness can belong to the soul as a sensing being or as an intellect. The first kind appears in people with vivid powers of imagination, such as a diviner or someone thought to have the evil eye. The second appears in people with great knowledge.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00325

A soul is noble by nature when it resembles higher, immaterial beings in wisdom and freedom. Wisdom may be inborn or learned. Inborn wisdom means that a person's judgments and beliefs tend to be true. This is the first natural capacity for developing learned wisdom. Human beings differ in this gift. The highest degree belongs to the holy, prophetic soul. The Qur'an describes it as oil that “almost gives light, even if no fire touches it.” This soul does not need a human teacher to gain knowledge. At the other extreme is a dull soul that gains nothing even from a teacher.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00326

Freedom means that the soul is not naturally obedient to bodily desires and the pleasures of animal life. A soul that obeys them is not free. In everyday language, freedom is the opposite of slavery. Desires can overpower and command incomplete souls, making them servants to their appetites whether or not they give in to them. A person who longs for something but cannot have it may be more troubled than one who has it now, even if the first person may fare better in the end. Turning away from what is desired may eventually lessen the longing.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00327

True freedom, then, is an inborn quality of the soul, not something produced by habit or teaching, though those too can help a person become virtuous. Aristotle calls freedom a settled quality that guards the soul from within, not a skill imposed on it from outside. In short, the weaker the soul's ties to the body and the stronger its ties to reason, the freer it is. The opposite makes it more enslaved to desire.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00328

Plato points to this when he says, “Base souls dwell in the realm of nature and its shadow; noble souls dwell in the realm of intellect.” If you understand wisdom and freedom, you can see that all the virtues of the soul come back to these two: a power to understand many things, and freedom from material attachments. The many bad traits likewise come back to their opposites. It is not enough to cleanse the soul of only some of them. If even one remains in control, it may draw the person toward the others. No one escapes their harm except the one who comes to God with a sound heart. God says, “Successful is the one who purifies the soul, and lost is the one who corrupts it.” The Prophet, peace be upon him and his family, said, “I was sent to perfect noble character.”
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00329

Just as a person's outward appearance is beautiful when all its parts are well formed and balanced, the inner self is beautiful only when all its parts are sound. Then good character, wisdom, and freedom can develop. The inner self has four powers: knowledge, anger, desire, and reason. Justice keeps them in balance. When these powers are balanced, the many traits of character that grow from them also fall into balance.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00330

The power of knowledge is at its best when it can tell truth from falsehood in speech, right from wrong in belief, and good from bad in action. When this power is balanced, without excess or neglect, it gives rise to wisdom. In truth, wisdom is the root of all good and the source of the other virtues. God says, “Whoever is given wisdom has been given much good.” He also says, “That is God's favor; He gives it to whom He wills. God is the possessor of great favor,” after saying that He teaches people the Book and wisdom. This wisdom—the knowledge of things as they are—is a fruit of the first kind, moral wisdom. The more knowledge a person gains, the better; this is not true of moral wisdom, which must remain balanced.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00331
Further note
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00332

The power of anger is balanced when it follows wisdom and religious law. The same is true of desire. Justice is the power that keeps anger and desire under the guidance of reason and religion. Theoretical reason is like a wise adviser. Justice is the power that carries out its instructions. Anger and desire are the powers that act on those instructions. They are like a hunting dog's and horse's movements: they should move, stop, hold back, or reach out when the guide directs them.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00333

A balanced power of anger is called courage. God loves the courageous. Excess becomes recklessness; deficiency becomes cowardice. Courage gives rise to generosity, bravery, self-respect, patience, steadiness, control of anger, dignity, and other good traits. Excessive anger gives rise to recklessness, arrogance, extravagance, rage, pride, and conceit. Too little anger gives rise to cowardice, humiliation, meanness, lack of concern for one's family, lack of protective feeling, and a small heart.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00334

A balanced power of desire is called chastity. Excess becomes greed; deficiency becomes dullness. Chastity gives rise to generosity, modesty, patience, forgiveness, contentment, piety, freedom from greed, and kindness. Excessive desire gives rise to greed, shamelessness, waste, hypocrisy, indecency, flattery, envy, delight in others' suffering, fawning on the rich, and looking down on the poor.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00335

A balanced power of reason gives rise to sound judgment and planning, a quick mind, good sense, and the ability to notice small details in people's actions and the hidden dangers in the soul. Excess becomes cunning and deceit. Deficiency becomes dullness, stupidity, foolishness, and gullibility.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00336

These are the main roots of good and bad character. The account of the hypocrite's punishment in the grave describes them as the four heads of a dragon. Good character in all four powers and in all the traits that grow from them means finding the middle ground between excess and deficiency. The best course is the middle one, and both extremes are blameworthy. God says, “Do not keep your hand chained to your neck, nor stretch it out completely.” He also says, “When they spend, they are neither wasteful nor stingy, but follow a course between the two,” and, “They are firm against the unbelievers and kind to one another.” If any one of these powers departs from the right course, good character is still incomplete.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00337

It is also important to know that strength of soul and nobility of soul are not the same thing. Each can be present without the other, though they sometimes come together. Courage, for example, may come from strength: a person looks down on an opponent and expects to defeat them. Or it may come from nobility: a person refuses to accept humiliation. A philosopher says, “Noble souls refuse to live in humiliation. They see that life in humiliation is death, and death in it is life.”
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00338

When courage comes from strength, it must also be guided by wisdom. Courage then means that the soul follows the sound judgment of reason in both acting and holding back. Cowardice follows reason in holding back, but not in acting. This may come from ignorance or weakness. Recklessness follows reason in acting, but not in holding back; it comes from strength without knowledge.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00339

A desire to rule may come from a noble soul or from a strong but ignorant one. The ignorant person mistakenly believes they deserve what is beyond their reach, and their strength drives them to seek it. Self-sufficiency may come from strength and confidence in one's ability to meet a need, or from nobility and a lack of attachment to present things or worry about what is absent. A feeling of poverty may come from weakness and fear of being without what one needs, or from baseness and greed. Justice belongs to a noble soul, especially when it is strong; injustice belongs to a low and grasping soul. Truthfulness goes with nobility, lying with baseness. Generosity comes from strength joined to nobility; foolishness from weakness joined to baseness. High ambition belongs to a strong and noble soul, while failure and small ambition belong to a weak and low one.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00340
Chapter 3 — The stages of a person, according to the powers of the soul
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00341

The inner self of every human being is a mixture of different powers: animal, predatory, devilish, and angelic. The animal power gives rise to appetite, greed, and unrestrained desire. The predatory power gives rise to envy, hostility, and hatred. The devilish power gives rise to cunning, deception, schemes, pride, the love of status, boasting, and the desire to dominate. The angelic power gives rise to knowledge and purity. These four are the roots from which all character grows. They are mixed together so deeply within a person that they are hard to separate.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00342

The soul escapes the darkness of the first three through the light of guidance that comes from reason and religious teaching. The animal power appears first in a child, bringing appetite and greed. Next the predatory power appears, bringing hostility and a tendency to quarrel. Then the devilish power takes hold. It first brings cunning and deception, as the animal and angry powers lead a person to use intelligence to satisfy desire and anger. Later it brings pride, conceit, boasting, and the desire to rise above others.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00343

After this, the intellect develops. It brings the light of faith. It belongs to God's side and to the angels; the other powers belong to Satan's forces. The intellect's growth is complete around the age of forty, though it begins to appear at puberty. The other powers have reached the heart before puberty. The soul grows familiar with them and follows their desires.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00344

When the light of the intellect arrives, a battle begins in the heart. If the intellect is weak, Satan takes control, and the person is gathered with Satan and all his forces. If the intellect grows strong through knowledge and faith, the other powers become subject to it and join the ranks of the angels. No soul knows in what land it will die.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00345
Chapter 4 — How perception rises from the lowest level to the highest
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00346

Know that every universal idea we understand has a nature that can be shared by many. Take human nature. Considered simply as human, it can belong to many people. By itself, it does not tell us whether there is one person or many, whether it is known through reason or sense, or whether it is universal or particular. If it did, it could not apply to the opposite case.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00347

When this nature exists in external matter, it comes with certain qualities, size, place, position, and time. These are not part of what it means to be human, but they are part of each person's particular way of existing. They help make that person an individual. Ordinary thinkers suppose that human nature exists outside the mind in one way, while its individual features have another existence. They do not understand the different ways existence can appear.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00348

In the world outside the mind, a human being exists as a particular individual with some size, qualities, place, and other features. These are not separate things added to the person's existence. People see that such features change while human nature remains and conclude that the person's existence is different from the nature of humanity. They miss that one nature can exist in many individuals without losing its unity as a kind or as an idea in the mind. A single person, too, can change from one state of existence to another while remaining the same individual through gradual, continuous change.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00349

Ancient philosophers wrote that the senses, imagination, inner judgment, and intellect arise as we leave behind different bodily conditions. People thought this meant that perception removes some features and leaves others behind. But every act of perception is a way of existing. The object moves from one level of existence to another while its nature and identity remain.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00350

A material thing exists with a particular matter, size, qualities, and place. A sense-image exists as a form with no physical place, but it depends on an outside object and a similar form in the sense. If the material object were absent, the sense would not receive its image.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00351
An imagined image, by contrast, does not depend on the continued presence of material.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00352
A sense-image arises only when something is sensed, and remains a particular image, not an idea that applies to many things.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00353

An image formed by imagination is still a particular image, not a general idea. An idea understood by the mind can apply to many individuals: the general idea of a human being, for example. The intellectual human being also has intellectual forms of hearing, sight, hands, and other organs. These many meanings do not divide the simple intellectual being, because one simple being can contain many different meanings.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00354

We have often explained that things with a nature move toward their perfection and purpose. Of all natural beings, the human being is special: one individual can rise from the lowest levels to the highest while remaining the same individual. Other natural things do not follow this path. The matter that carries their form takes on another kind of form, separate from the one it had before; it does not preserve either the individual or the kind.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00355

A human being, by contrast, can have several modes of existence: bodily, imaginal, and intellectual. Each has many levels—not an endless number of separate things outside the mind, but levels we can distinguish in thought. The person moves from a lower level to a higher one, from a less complete state to a nobler one. The person completes the stages of one mode of existence before passing to the next.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00356

From childhood until bodily maturity, a person is first a bodily human being. As this mode of existence develops, it becomes clearer and finer, until the person gains imaginal existence, the second human being. This imaginal human being has its own organs, but they do not need to occupy separate places as bodily organs do. In the bodily world, sight and hearing need different organs. Taste and smell also need different organs. Some powers are more divided and depend more on matter than others. Touch is the lowest level of animal life, so every animal has it, even one as low as a shellfish or worm. In the imaginal human being, the senses are gathered together in one inner sense.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00357

The powers that move the body are also spread across different organs: some are in the liver, some in the brain, some in the heart, some in the reproductive organs, and others elsewhere. In the imaginal human being, they are gathered together. If a person—rarely—rises from this imaginal existence to the intellectual level and becomes an active intellect, they are an intellectual human being, the third human being, with intellectual organs as we have said.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00358

Looking up from this world, the order is bodily, imaginal, and intellectual. Looking down from the world of intellect, the order is reversed. Aristotle's Theology says that the first, intellectual human gives its light to the second, imaginal human being, who in turn gives light to the third, bodily human. So the bodily human contains the meanings of both the imaginal and intellectual human, but only faintly. It is an image of an image.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00359

There is no contradiction between saying that some people rise from bodily existence to imaginal existence and, in rare cases, intellectual existence, and saying that the bodily human contains both higher meanings. The first statement is about what has become actual in a person, not about a connection that remains only as a possibility.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00360

A human being is the soul and body together. Though they differ in rank, they exist as one being with two ends: one changes and passes away like a branch, while the other remains like a root. As the soul becomes more complete, the body becomes finer and clearer, more closely joined to the soul, and more united with it. When the intellectual level is reached, the two become one without distinction.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00361

People generally think that, when the soul changes from its worldly state to its afterlife state, it leaves the body behind like someone taking off clothes. They think the body it managed and moved was the corpse left after death. This is wrong. The dead body is no longer the thing the soul manages directly. It is like waste or sediment cast off by the body's processes, or like hair, wool, horns, and hooves that nature produces outside the living body's essential activity. It is like a house built to protect someone from heat and cold—useful in this world, but not itself alive.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00362

The true body is the one in which sensation and life flow as part of its very being, not by accident. Its relation to the soul is like the relation of light to the sun. When the soul reaches a higher level, it is like an object that has become sensed, then imagined, then understood. Abstraction does not mean that some features are removed and others kept. It means that the object's lower, darker existence changes into a higher, brighter, and more complete one. In the same way, the human being's passage from this world to the next is a change from one mode of existence to another.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00363

The soul does not become an intellect by losing some powers, such as sensation, while keeping others, such as reason. As its existence grows stronger and more complete, all its powers grow stronger and more complete with it. The higher it rises, the less divided it is and the more unified it becomes.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00364

Aristotle supports this account. He says that the first human being is sensitive, but in a higher and better way than the lower human being. The lower human being receives its senses from the human being in the higher intellectual world. The higher one does not receive anything from the lower; instead, the lower depends on the higher.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00365

The senses and the things perceived in the higher world are not bodies. Nor does the higher human being see and sense in the same way we do. Its senses are stronger and reach more things because they perceive what is nobler, clearer, and more complete. Its sight understands what many beings share, while our bodily sight sees individual things. Our sight is weaker because it sees lesser things: bodily images of those higher realities. As Aristotle says, “These senses are weak intellects, and those intellects are strong senses.”
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00366

Aristotle also says that if the soul contains the forms of active causes, the human soul contains the sources of life and speech. A soul that exists in this way before entering a body is already a human being there. When it enters a body, it becomes the image of another human being, as much as that body can receive. It is like a sculptor making a human figure from material, trying to make it resemble a real person. The figure is only an image. It does not have the true person's powers, life, movement, states, or abilities.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00367

In the same way, the bodily human being is an image of the first, true human being. But here the sculptor is the soul. It makes the bodily human resemble the true one, though the body's human qualities are weak and faint. The true human being's powers and life are strong. If you want to see the first, true human being, you must be good and virtuous, and have senses strong enough not to shrink from the bright lights shining upon them.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00368

This is the human being Plato describes in the teaching of divine forms. He says there are two human beings: one that can be sensed and will perish, and one that is lasting and never disappears. But Aristotle adds to this account by saying that the true human being uses the body and acts through bodily tools. What this means is that the soul uses the body indirectly, through the animal soul, not as its first and direct means. When the animal soul reaches the imaginal world, the rational soul follows it and gives it a higher, more noble life. The rational soul does not leave the intellectual world to descend; it remains connected to this life from above.
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00369
Someone might object: if the soul in the higher world can sense, how can sensation belong to noble, higher beings when it also belongs to lower beings?
Book Nine — The human soul's traits, actions, reactions, and stages
passage-en-00370

We answer that sensation in the higher, intellectual world is not like sensation in this lower world. The higher being senses according to the kinds of things that exist there. Its sight is connected to the sight of the lower human being, as one fire is connected to another higher fire. The lower human being receives the power of sense through this connection. If there were bodies in the higher world like these bodies here, the higher soul would sense them too. The second human—the image of the first in the bodily world—senses bodies because it carries traces of the first human being's intellectual form.
